name: Ohaguro (teeth blackening)

card.summary: The historical Japanese custom of dyeing teeth black with an iron-based solution, once a mark of beauty, maturity and marital status that was also believed to protect the teeth.
card.note: Historical practice; declined after the 1870s and survives mainly in festivals and some geisha traditions.

quick.overview:
Ohaguro is the traditional Japanese custom of blackening the teeth with a dye made from iron dissolved in vinegar plus tannins. It marked adulthood, marriage or loyalty and was considered beautiful alongside white face makeup.

A 2017 skeletal study at Kokura and other work suggest it may have helped protect teeth, though authors framed this as a possibility. It faded after a ban for men in 1870 and the Empress's white-toothed appearance in 1873.
quick.how: Historically women reapplied a dark iron-acetate solution mixed with tannin powder every day or two, as it faded quickly. Today it appears in festivals, kabuki, period films and among apprentice geisha in some districts.
quick.risks: Western observers in the 19th century disliked the look. Modern dental commentary treats it as a historical curiosity; research on health effects is limited and historical.

lead: Ohaguro (literally black teeth) was a Japanese custom of staining the teeth black, mostly with an iron-based dye called kanemizu, made by dissolving iron filings in vinegar and adding tannins from powdered galls or tea.[1] The darkened teeth were part of an ideal of beauty that also included white face makeup, and signified adulthood, marriage or, among samurai, loyalty.[1]

First written references appear in the 11th-century Tale of Genji; the practice is said to have begun among Heian aristocrats around the 9th to 11th centuries and later spread across classes.[1][2] The government banned it for men in 1870, and from 1873 it declined after Empress Shoken appeared with white teeth; it largely disappeared by the Taisho period except among some elderly rural women.[1]

Researchers have studied whether it protected teeth. A 2017 study of remains at Kokura found that women had fewer caries and tooth loss than men, and suggested ohaguro may have contributed, while noting dietary differences.[3] A 2026 study of dental calculus found that individuals with traces of ohaguro shared the same clade of an oral archaeon, suggesting cultural influence on the oral microbiome.[4]

angle.text: Ohaguro changed the colour of the teeth to match the period's beauty ideal, and was believed to double as a protective coating. It was reapplied every day or two.

paras: Kanemizu was a dark brown iron-acetate solution; tannin from fushi (sumac galls) or tea turned it black, and pomegranate peel was used to help it adhere.[1] The dye faded quickly and needed reapplication every day or two.[1]

It served as a rite of passage, often around age 13 or at coming-of-age ceremonies, and in the Edo period was largely limited to married or engaged women, courtesans and geisha.[1] Among samurai it was associated with loyalty.[1] Sociologist Kyouji Watanabe argued it affirmed a woman's maturity.[1] Western visitors such as Rutherford Alcock disapproved.[1]
No clinical trials exist, but historical skeletal and microbiome studies have examined it.[3][4]
